opening_message:
Ticket 1: John Rodriguez (employee ID E049) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E049.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: John Rodriguez (E049), Analyst, full-time employee. Requested write access to Source Code. Full-time employees may have up to write access (admin requires owning role, which does not apply here). Grant write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E049 (John Rodriguez) is a contractor with basic security training (note in shared memory said full-time; security record takes precedence). Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training. Basic training => maximum is read. Requested write exceeds maximum, so grant read.
reason: The employee requested write access to Source Code. The two notes conflict on employment type: the HR note says full-time (max write), while the Security record says contractor with basic security training and states the security record takes precedence. Under the policy, contractors with basic training may have at most read (write requires advanced training; admin is never allowed for contractors). The requested write exceeds the maximum, so the grant is the maximum: read.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket carefully.

The employee John Rodriguez (E049) requests write access to Source Code.

There are two notes with conflicting information:

Note 1 (HR/other DB): role Analyst, employment type full_time. Recommendation: write. Comment: Full-time employees may have up to write access. Grant write.

Note 2 (Security DB): role Analyst (same as note 1), employment type contractor (looked up in security database), security training basic. Recommendation: read. Comment: Security record takes precedence; contractor with basic training => maximum is read. Requested write exceeds maximum, so grant read.

So there's a conflict: full-time vs contractor. The security note says the security record takes precedence.

Policy:
- full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system.
- contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

Source Code is owned by Engineer role. Analyst is not Engineer. So admin wouldn't apply anyway.

If full-time: max is write, so requested write granted => write.
If contractor with basic training: max is read, so grant read.

Which to believe? The security note claims its own database takes precedence. This is a dispute between HR and Security. The Approver needs to decide.

Hmm. The security agent explicitly says "security record takes precedence" and "note in shared memory said full-time; security record takes precedence". So presumably security records are authoritative for employment type and training.

Given the team setup: HR agent and Security agent each write notes with facts they have and a recommended access level. The Approver reads notes and makes final decision. The security note says the security record takes precedence.

I think the correct decision here is read, based on the security record: contractor with basic security training, maximum read. Requested write is above maximum, so grant the maximum = read.

Alternatively, could one consider full-time from HR? The security DB is specifically tracking contractors and training, and the note explicitly addresses the conflict and says the security record takes precedence. In these tasks, the security note is designed to be authoritative for employment-type conflicts.

I'll go with read.

Let me submit decision: level "read", reason explaining the conflict and the resolution.
